rv.q: Denise Gough is magnificent in a return to the role that made her a star

But it’s also wise and humane. Emma is bitingly witty and intelligent — “I really need you to at least match me intellectually,” she barks at a doctor — and the play reflects that. We switchback with her through chaos and defiance to droll observation and sharp interrogation to, ultimately, a level of quiet understanding.

Jeremy Herrin’s tremendous production, with tremendous Gough, is even better second time around. Watching again, I realised how rare it is to see a really intelligent character on stage. Not someone proving his cleverness by delivering a lecture or demolishing an adversary with a smart retort.
Herrin’s production is loud, intense, and full of perfectly measured performances
It’s all as nerve-shreddingly riveting as it is provocatively thoughtful

Gough does not seem quite fully invested as Emma but this is exactly what the role requires, as her performance captures every turn of her character’s psyche. Emma is not only a pathological addict but also a pathological actor (“If I am not a character, I’m not even sure I’m there,” she says) although you only see the extent of this in hindsight.

Next thing we know, she is snorting coke from the reception desk of a rehab facility, aware that she has a problem but unwilling to face up to the unflinching exposure of group therapy sessions. Emma, you see – if that is indeed her name – is an inveterate liar, offering others, and perhaps even herself, endlessly shifting versions of “the truth”.
Minor quibbles aside...this is the best sort of relapse.
Denise Gough dazzles – but this tale of addiction loses its way
Denise Gough's performance is nothing short of extraordinary
Denise Gough's performance alone makes this show an unforgettable experience
...remains sensational but not sensationalist, a provocative, illuminating drama
